activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Setting an account to private limits who can see your posts, but anyone you have already accepted as a follower can still copy or share what they see.
story:
Landon hunched over the family computer, refreshing his feed for the tenth time. The photo he had posted last night, a shot of his new mountain bike leaning against the garage, should have been safe. His account was private, so only people he had accepted could see it. Yet there it was on a public page called "Bike Spots of Riverside," his bike, his garage door, and the corner of his street sign just visible behind the spokes.

"Maya, come look at this," he said.

His sister wandered in with her phone in one hand and a rice cake in the other. Maya wanted one thing above all else this summer, which was to reach a thousand followers so she could feel like a real artist instead of a kid with a sketchbook. She leaned over his shoulder and frowned at the screen.

"That's your garage," she said. "How did it get on a public page?"

"That's what I want to know." Landon scrolled down. The repost had a caption: "Found this beauty parked on Maple Court, near the school." His stomach tightened. Whoever posted it knew his street.

Maya sat on the edge of the desk chair. "You accepted that guy last week, didn't you? Dev something. He commented on my drawings once."

Landon remembered, and the memory rose up like a flashback from a movie. It was the night he'd gotten the bike, and he'd been so proud that he'd accepted three follow requests in a row without checking any of them. Dev had a profile picture of a skate park and zero posts of his own. Landon had tapped accept in half a second, thinking only that more followers made his page look good, the way Maya was always saying it did.

"I barely know him," Landon said slowly. "But he's a follower, so he can see everything I post." He stopped, turning the idea over. "And if he can see it, he can copy it. Private just means strangers can't walk in the door. It doesn't stop people already inside from carrying things out."

"Ugh," Maya said. "That's like a parasite. It latches on and takes stuff, and you don't even notice."

Landon wasn't ready to accuse anyone yet. He wanted proof, not a guess. So he tried a test, the way his science teacher liked to say, one variable at a time. He posted a new photo of the bike with a caption that read, "Moving the bike to my grandma's porch on Delmore Road for the week." Delmore Road was a real street, but his grandma lived two towns away. If Dev was the one leaking, the leak would follow the fake trail.

The waiting was the worst part. Landon refreshed the page every few minutes, his knee bouncing under the desk. Maya stood behind him, chewing her rice cake down to nothing. The afternoon light shifted across the keyboard. Finally, a new post appeared on Bike Spots of Riverside: Landon's photo, with a caption that said, "This one's hiding out on Delmore now. Grandmas keep the best bikes."

Maya gasped. Landon felt something cold slide through him. Nobody knew about Delmore except his followers, and only one of them had a page full of other people's photos, all reposted, all tagged with locations, as if collecting kids' stuff was a hobby.

Landon clicked to his follower list, found Dev, and removed him. Then he went through every other name, evading the temptation to keep the ones that made his numbers look big, and removed anyone he couldn't say hello to in person. Maya watched him do it, quiet for once.

"I'm not going to accept randoms anymore either," she said at last, sounding more assertive than Landon had ever heard her. "A thousand followers isn't worth it if one of them is a thief."

She held up her phone to show him her sketchbook page, and the follower count sitting at 997.

"Three to go," she said, "but real ones this time."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japanese homes, shoes are taken off in an entrance area called the genkan before stepping inside.
story:
Ruby sprinted up the driveway with the gift bag swinging from her wrist, because Aunt Hana's dinner started at six o'clock sharp and it was already 5:54. Her mother had sent her ahead with the mangoes while the rest of the family piled out of the minivan, arguing about parking.

At the front door, Ruby stopped so fast she nearly skidded. The porch light showed a neat row of shoes beside the step, all toes pointing outward, and beyond them a lower floor of dark tile inside the doorway. Two pairs of slippers sat waiting on the raised hallway floor, as if they had been set out on purpose.

"That's the genkan," said her cousin Kenta, popping his head around the door. "You take your shoes off there before you come in."

Ruby peeled off her sneakers and lined them up with the others, matching the direction. Then she stepped up in her socks and slid her feet into the slippers, which were a half size too big but felt weirdly official, like a costume. Kenta grinned and led her toward the kitchen, where the smell of grilled fish had taken over the whole house like it owned the place.

"Careful with those," Kenta said, nodding at her bag. "The wrapping paper Aunt Hana likes is kind of flammable, so keep it away from the stove." Ruby clutched the bag tighter. She had learned about wrapping at Grandma's last Thanksgiving, where you handed gifts over with both hands and the receiver set them aside unopened, which had nearly eliminated Ruby's ability to wait, but she had survived. Here, apparently, the mangoes would be presented before dinner, so she had that to look forward to.

At the table, Ruby noticed Kenta saying "itadakimasu" before anyone touched the chopsticks, so she said it too, copying his rhythm, and Aunt Hana beamed at her like she had won something. Then Ruby watched how Kenta held his bowl close to his chin and never stuck his chopsticks upright into his rice, and she decided to test a theory: if she copied him move for move, nobody would correct her once all evening. Bowl up, chopsticks low, quiet slurp of the noodles, which at her own house would have earned her a look from her father but here got Aunt Hana an approving nod at both of them.

"Second helping?" Aunt Hana asked, already reaching for the pot.

"Yes, please," Ruby said, lifting her bowl with both hands.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Psychologist Thomas Gordon coined the term 'I-message' in the 1960s: a sentence like 'I felt left out' describes the speaker's feelings instead of blaming the listener with 'you'.
story:
The bus lurched around the corner before Logan even reached his seat, and he grabbed the rail so hard his knuckles went white. Four rows back, Dex was laughing with Marcus Chen about something on Marcus's phone. Something that had happened Saturday, apparently, at the skate park. The skate park where Logan had stood alone for forty minutes, checking the entrance, before texting are you coming? and getting nothing.

"Move it, Day," said a sixth grader, and Logan slid into the seat across the aisle, backpack first. He yanked out his notebook, the one with the torn cover, and flipped past his math homework to a blank page. He was going to write it down. The whole thing. And then he was going to say it out loud, tomorrow, in the cafeteria, before his courage restricted itself to zero.

He wrote fast: You ditched me Saturday. You never even texted back. You like Marcus better now. He read it back and his stomach dropped, because even on paper it sounded like an accusation, and Dex had a reputation for shutting down the second anyone came at him. One time in third grade a kid called Dex a cheater at four square and Dex didn't talk to him for a month.

Then Logan remembered something. Last year, rainy Tuesday, library, hiding in the self-help shelf because Ms. Perrin had sent him there during indoor recess. He'd pulled down a dusty orange book just for something to read, and it had said that a psychologist named Thomas Gordon coined the term "I-message" back in the 1960s. The idea was a sentence like "I felt left out" described the speaker's own feelings instead of blaming the listener with "you." Logan had thought it was boring then. Now it felt like a combination he'd been given for a lock he'd been kicking for three days.

He crossed out every you. He wrote: I felt left out on Saturday. I waited and I felt like I didn't matter. It still said the same true thing, but it didn't point a finger. It just opened a door. He copied it onto his hand in pen, where he couldn't lose it, and the bus hissed to a stop at the corner of Fitch Street.

Dex was getting off at this stop too. Logan's heart hammered like he was about to drop in on a half-pipe. "Dex!" he called, squeezing past the sixth grader. "Wait up. One second." He caught him at the mailbox, held out his ink-covered hand like evidence, and read it, fast, before Dex's face could close: "I felt left out on Saturday. I felt like I didn't matter to you anymore."

Dex stared at the ink. "My phone died at my grandma's," he said. "Then my mom restricted me from the park for the weekend because of my grades. I was going to tell you Monday but Marcus made it sound like the best day ever and it got weird." He kicked a pebble off the curb. "You want to come over today? We still haven't landed the stair drop."

"Race you to your door," said Logan, and ran.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Most vegetable seeds need water, oxygen and warmth to germinate, but not light; a few, such as lettuce, sprout better with light and are sown very shallowly.
story:
Arthur wanted lettuce more than anything else in the garden, because Grandpa's sandwich bread came from the bakery two towns over and the tomatoes were already coming, and lettuce was the missing piece. He measured out three beds behind Grandpa's shed, turned the soil with a fork, and planted one bed with beans pushed deep, one bed with lettuce pushed just as deep, and one bed with lettuce scattered on top of the dirt and patted down.

Every morning he watered all three beds and pressed his palm flat on the soil to feel the warmth. "You're very optimistic about that third bed," Grandpa said from the porch, watching him pat seeds he could barely see. "That's not even planting. That's seasoning."

Nine days later the beans were up in two crooked rows, fat and green. The deep lettuce bed was bare, not one sprout, and Arthur got down on his knees and dug where he remembered placing the seeds. He found them, swollen and pale and going nowhere. The shallow bed had a fuzz of green across the whole surface, tiny leaves lifting like they were stretching.

He sat back on his heels and thought about the pattern. Beans had gone deep and sprouted. Lettuce had gone deep and failed. The difference couldn't be the water, because he had watered everything the same, and it couldn't be warmth, because the dirt was warm everywhere he checked. That implied the depth itself was the thing. But depth meant one thing above all: how much light reached the seed. The beans had come up from the dark without any trouble, so dark wasn't the problem for beans. Maybe lettuce was the opposite kind of seed, a category that needed light to sprout at all, which would mean it had to sit almost on top of the soil to get any.

He tried it again to be sure. He filled two trays on the windowsill. In the first he set lettuce seeds on the surface of damp soil. In the second he buried them half an inch down, then put a shoebox over the tray so it stayed dark but just as warm and just as wet. The surface tray greened up in five days. The covered tray stayed empty until Arthur lifted the box, and then only the two seeds nearest the edge, where a stripe of sun had crept in, put up leaves.

"Beans don't care," he told Grandpa, laying the two trays side by side on the porch table. "Give them water and warm dirt and air, and they'd come up in a coal cellar. But lettuce wants the light on it, so you basically just set the seeds down and dust them over."

Grandpa leaned in and looked at the two trays, then at the green fuzz of the third bed glowing in the evening field.

"Sandwiches in three weeks," he said, and went inside to start the tomatoes.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: A glow stick shines brighter but runs out faster when it is warm, and glows dimmer but lasts longer when it is cold.
story:
Theodore sat in the back seat with the glow stick in his fist, trying to look like this was no big deal. Dad drove, Mom checked her mirror every few blocks like a bird watching a migratory flock cross the highway, and the gymnasium lights got closer with every turn.

"Crack it now," Mom said. "It'll be brighter by the time you walk in."

That was the problem. Theodore had cracked his glow stick two nights ago, testing it in his room, and it had already burned half its glow. His best friend Marcus had cracked his the same night, and both sticks had come from the same pack. Marcus's had died completely by morning. Theodore's was still going, but faintly, like a firefly that was getting tired.

He turned the stick over in his hand. Both sticks, same pack, same night. Marcus had kept his in the pocket of a hoodie hanging next to the radiator, the warmest spot in his room. Theodore had left his on the windowsill, where the night air leaked through the old frame. Warm stick, dead by morning. Cold stick, still glowing. He had tested it again with a third stick from the pack, one he'd held against the heater vent for ten minutes after cracking it. That one had blazed like a tiny green flare, brighter than either of theirs had ever been, and it had gone dark before dinner.

So there was a rule hiding in there somewhere. A warm stick shone brighter but ran out faster. A cold one glowed dimmer but lasted longer. If that was true, then tonight the bright sticks everyone else was cracking in the parking lot would be gorgeous for an hour and then nothing. His dim stick, if he kept it cold until the last song, might be the only one still alive.

"Variable," he said out loud, then felt his ears go red.

"What was that?" Dad asked.

"Nothing. Can you turn the AC toward the back?"

"It's forty degrees out, Theo."

"Please. It's for a science thing." That was almost true. He wrapped the glow stick in a napkin and pressed it against the cold air from the vent, budgeting its glow like the last pieces of a candy bar, saving everything for the end of the night. Mom and Dad exchanged a look in the front seat, the kind that said they knew something he hadn't figured out yet, but neither of them said it.

The gym was loud and hot and flashing. Theodore danced badly with Priya from science class, spilled punch on his own shoe, and watched, song by song, as the gym went dark in patches. First the bright orange sticks faded, then the blue ones, and by the time the slow songs started, half the kids were holding dead plastic tubes and complaining about it. When the last song began, Theodore slipped out to the car, unwrapped his stick from the napkin, and cupped it in his hands.

It was still glowing. Faint, green, stubborn, alive.

He walked back through the double doors holding it up, and Priya turned around first. Her own stick had gone black an hour ago.

"How is yours still going?" she asked. "Mine died forever ago."

"Trade secret," Theodore said. "But if you put yours somewhere cold tonight, you can find out in the morning."

"Like where?"

"The freezer," he said. "Meet me at the bus stop. If yours glows even a little, you owe me a pudding cup."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A layer of mulch, such as straw or wood chips, keeps soil moist, blocks weeds from sprouting and evens out soil temperature.
story:
Colton had claimed plot fourteen at the community garden because it was the sunniest one, and he had big plans for it: three rows of carrots, two tomato plants, and a zucchini he privately intended to grow to the size of a small dog. His best friend Nadia had claimed plot fifteen, right beside his, mostly so they could argue across the fence without shouting.

Three weeks after planting, the trouble started. Colton's bed had been watered the same day as Nadia's, by the same sprinkler, but by Friday his soil had cracked into a brown checkerboard while hers stayed dark and damp. Worse, little green weed sprouts were popping up all over his rows like uninvited guests at a birthday party. Nadia leaned on the fence and grinned. "Did you plant weeds on purpose? Because they're thriving."

"I didn't plant anything," Colton said, kneeling down. He pressed a finger into her soil, then into his. Hers gave. His did not. He looked from one bed to the other, and the only difference he could see was the fluffy yellow layer of straw spread across hers like a blanket. "That's the mulch Mr. Ruiz gave you, isn't it."

"It's called mulch," Nadia said. "Straw or wood chips, either kind works."

Colton ran a hand over the straw. Underneath, her soil was cool and soft. His was baking in the sun. He borrowed a wheelbarrow, begged two bales of straw off Mr. Ruiz, and spread a layer over his whole bed, tucking it around the carrot seedlings like he was putting them to bed. "Enjoy your monarchy while it lasts," he told the weeds, "because your reign ends today."

Nadia snorted. "Weeds don't have a monarchy."

"Everything with that many subjects has a monarchy," Colton said. "I'm staging a rebellion."

The following week proved him right. When he pulled back a corner of the straw, his soil was damp, his carrots stood in straight little lines, and the only weeds he found were a few stubborn survivors pushing up at the very edge. He plucked those and dropped them over the fence into Nadia's compost bucket, one by one, like trophies.

At the fall harvest, Mr. Ruiz walked the rows with his clipboard and stopped at Colton's zucchini, which had grown to the size of a loaf of bread and was still going. "Now that's authentic gardening," he said. "You want to enter it in the fair?"

"Enter it?" Colton lifted the zucchini with both hands. "I'm going to name it King Mulch the First."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Streaming video uses far more mobile data than sending text messages, so watching videos away from Wi-Fi can use up a data plan quickly.
story:
The box was small, but Hudson's hands shook a little anyway. Inside was his first phone, dark and cool, with a screen that lit up before he even touched it. His mother had one rule, delivered while stirring soup that smelled of garlic and onions: "The family group chat is free over Wi-Fi, and the plan gives us a shared bucket of mobile data each month. Don't drain the bucket."

By Thursday, the bucket was nearly empty. Hudson knew this because his father sent a screenshot to the group chat with a single emoji, the one with the wide eyes. The numbers showed the family had used almost everything, and the month had a whole three weeks left. Hudson had only done one thing differently: every morning on the bus, he had watched videos while the heater rattled and the windows fogged up around the edges.

He sat on his bed and thought. His sister Zoe had texted constantly all week, hundreds of messages, and her name barely showed up in the usage numbers. He had watched maybe an hour of video total. Something was distinct about his phone use, something invisible. He scrolled back through the chat, counting her messages against the tiny data they used, and the pattern jumped out at him. Texts were like whispering. Video must be like shouting through a megaphone.

He decided to test it. "New plan," he typed into the group chat. "Texts only until the first of the month. No videos unless we're home on Wi-Fi." Zoe replied with a thumbs up and "finally, scientist Hudson." For a week he rode the bus with the phone in his pocket, feeling it buzz with messages, reading them instead of watching anything. He learned to compress his jokes into short texts, because "the dog ate my entire sandwich and also my homework" was funnier than three paragraphs anyway.

When the new month started, his father posted fresh numbers in the chat. With everyone texting instead of streaming away from home, the data bucket barely rippled. "Whatever you did," his father wrote, "keep doing it." Hudson grinned and typed back, "Videos eat data like Zoe eats popcorn. Texts barely take a crumb."

Zoz replied with a photo of an empty popcorn bowl and the words "Rude but accurate." Then, because the family was home and on Wi-Fi, they all pressed play at the same time on the same video, and in three different rooms of the house, the same laugh started up at the same moment.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Hormones in puberty make oil glands in the skin produce more oil, called sebum, which can clog pores and lead to acne.
story:
Carter sat in the waiting room of Dr. Okafor's office, holding his phone low so his mom wouldn't see, typing to Nadia, who had texted him from the pharmacy across the street.

"Guess what I found out," Nadia wrote. "I'm comparing face washes. There's a whole aisle. My forehead started breaking out this year and I wanted to know why, so I read the labels and looked it up. Hormones in puberty make the oil glands in your skin produce more oil. It's called sebum. The extra oil can clog your pores, and that's what leads to acne."

Carter stared at the message. So it wasn't because he'd skipped washing his face after soccer on Tuesday, which was what he'd decided at 2 a.m. last night while poking at the red bump above his eyebrow. Hormones. Things happening inside him that nobody could see, sending instructions to his skin like a radio station broadcasting to a city. He wondered what else the station was telling his body to do without asking him first.

"That's why washing more doesn't fix it," he typed back. "I've been scrubbing like it's dirt. It's not dirt. It's my own skin making too much oil."

"It's not an illusion, it's chemistry," Nadia replied. "Also there are like forty washes and they all say equivalent results on the bottle, which I doubt. Pick your book up, your mom says you're daydreaming."

He shoved the phone in his pocket. His name was called, and he followed the nurse down the hall, past a poster showing cross-sections of skin. In the exam room, Dr. Okafor looked at the bump, then at Carter's chart, then asked him a question that surprised him. "What do you think caused it?"

Carter explained, careful to get it right. Puberty, hormones, oil glands, more oil, clogged pores. Dr. Okafor smiled a little. "Where'd you learn that?"

"My friend Nadia. She was at the pharmacy."

"Well, she did her homework, and so did you." The doctor turned the light toward Carter's eyebrow again. "Here's the thing, though. That's not acne."

"It's not?"

"That's a small cyst, completely harmless, and it's going away on its own. But the acne is coming, Carter, probably starting this winter. Your feet grew two sizes in four months, your voice is doing interesting things, and bacteria that cause breakouts? They thrive right where you're headed. So let's talk about what actually works, and it's a lot easier than scrubbing."

Carter leaned forward. "Wait, say the easy part first."

Dr. Okafor pulled a sample bottle from the drawer and dropped it in Carter's hand. "Wash gently, once a day, with this."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Details in the background of a photo, such as a street sign, a house number or a school logo, can let a stranger work out where it was taken.
story:
Nicholas had one job before lunch: pick the photo for the robotics team's page. He scrolled through the folder on the lab computer while his friend Dex leaned over his shoulder, chewing a straw like it owed him money.

"Use the one with the robot's arm up," Dex said. "That looks awesome."

"That's the one where I dropped a piston on my foot," Nicholas said. "Look, I'm mid-hop. Nobody needs to see that." The robot itself was fine. They'd spent three weeks getting the little engine part to pump up and down, and yesterday the arm had finally moved fast enough to make Dex's little brother scream and run in a circle.

They settled on a selfie: Nicholas, Dex, and Priya on Priya's front porch, the robot held up between them like a trophy. Priya was grinning so hard her eyes were closed. Nicholas hit upload, then paused, because something about the photo itched at him. He zoomed in, dragging the image bigger until it blurred.

"What now?" Dex asked.

"Zoom out before my retinas file a complaint." But Nicholas kept going. Behind Priya's head, on the porch railing, sat a little brass number. He traced it with his finger on the screen. Her house number. And over her shoulder, the corner of a green street sign stuck into the frame.

"So?" Dex said.

"So I know her address," Nicholas said slowly. "And we're about to post this where anybody can look at it. Anybody." He thought about how he'd once found a stranger's video and figured out the kid's school just from a logo on a gym banner in the background, and how he'd felt clever, then sort of slimy.

Priya appeared behind them with a juice box. "Why are you staring at my nostrils?"

"Your nostrils are safe," Nicholas said. "Your house isn't. Somebody could zoom in on your house number and that street sign and know exactly where you live." He demonstrated, zooming until the brass numbers filled the screen like glowing digits of doom.

Priya squinted. "Huh. Okay, that's creepy."

"It's fixable," Nicholas said. He tried cropping. That cut off the robot. He tried smudging the number with the blur tool, which made the railing look like it was melting. Dex suggested drawing a mustache over the street sign, which, honestly, was tempting. Finally Nicholas angled it: they went back to Priya's porch after school, took the same photo at the bottom of the steps instead, porch rail and street sign behind the camera, and reposted it.

The new picture got forty likes by dinner. Dex commented, "Team Not-Kidnapped." Priya replied with a robot emoji, immune to his nonsense after three years of robotics club. The next morning, Mr. Alvarez paused at their lab table on his way past.

"Nice post," he said. "Clean frame, too."

Nicholas grinned and opened the folder for next week's photo. "Rule one," he said, dragging the zoom slider out to full, "we check everything at maximum magnification."

"Even my nostrils?" Priya asked.

"Especially your nostrils."

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: An emergency dispatcher usually first asks for the address of the emergency, so a babysitter should know the exact address of the house they are in.
story:
Owen stood on the Hendersons' back porch with a sticky note in his hand, copying the street address off a letter that sat on the kitchen counter. Mrs. Henderson had her keys out and one foot in her car already, because she and her husband had a long commute to the dinner where she worked, but Owen had remembered something from the babysitting class at the community center. The instructor had said that when you call for help in an emergency, the dispatcher usually asks for the address first, before anything else, so a babysitter should always know the exact address of the house. Owen had gotten that wrong once, on a quiz, and he had never forgotten it. So he wrote 42 Maple Court on his note and taped it next to the phone, just in case.

The little girl he was watching, Priya, was four, and she wanted to be in the backyard immediately. She wore a synthetic superhero cape that made a loud swishing sound when she ran, and she ran a lot. "I'm saving the ants," she announced, crouching by the fence with a magnifying glass. "This one's hurt." Owen knelt beside her. The ant was dragging a crumb and moving fine, but Priya pointed at a spot on its back. "It has a microbe," she said solemnly. Owen had learned about microbes in science, tiny living things too small to see, and he told her that was probably just dirt. She considered this, then decided the ant needed a hospital made from a flowerpot.

They built the hospital. They dug a small hospital sign into the dirt with a spoon. Priya decided the doctor was a pebble. It was going well until she stood up too fast, tripped over the flowerpot, and landed hard on the gravel border. There was a moment of silence, the worst kind, and then a cut above her eyebrow started bleeding and she cried in a scared, gulping way that made Owen's chest go tight.

He carried her inside, pressed a clean towel against the cut the way the class had taught him, and looked at the bleeding and at her pale face. It was longer than a bandage could hold, and he thought it might need stitches. His hands wanted to shake, but he made himself pick up the phone. He dialed the emergency number and said, "Forty-two Maple Court. That's the address of the emergency. A little girl cut her head and she's awake." The dispatcher's voice was calm and steady, and she asked her questions next, and an ambulance came with its lights quiet, no siren.

Mrs. Henderson sent Owen a letter two days later, because she said he wrote things down and she did too. "Priya got three stitches and a popsicle," she wrote. "She told the doctor her ant was also hurt and needed a bed. You called in the address before anything else, and the paramedics said that saved time when it mattered. You will babysit for us whenever you want, and Priya has already asked if the pebble doctor can come too."

The next Saturday, Owen was back in the same backyard, and the flowerpot hospital was still standing in the grass, a little crooked. Priya ran up in her swishing cape with a bandage above her eyebrow and held out her magnifying glass. "New patient," she said, pointing at a beetle. "This one's a big one."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In March 1933, Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda.
story:
Austin first noticed the ad during math homework, when his phone buzzed three times in a row. The group chat, Titans Forever, had gone from weekend plans to something called Vortex Fuel, a sports drink everyone suddenly had to try. Dev sent a photo of himself holding a can. Then Marcus. Then four other guys in a row, each one typing "everyone's switching" or "you're the only one left, Austin."

He typed back a question mark and got a wall of replies. The messages called the drink "legendary," "insane," "the future." One guy pasted a clip of a basketball player Austin had never heard of saying Vortex Fuel was the only thing he trusted. The chat moved so fast that Austin felt like the last kid on earth who hadn't bought one.

The next morning at school, Mrs. Okafor's class took the bus to the history museum for the World War II unit. Austin trailed behind Dev and Marcus, still hearing about Vortex Fuel, until the class stopped in front of a wall of old posters. One showed a crowd of smiling workers, all marching the same direction. Another used glowing words like "strong," "pure," and "betrayal" for anyone who disagreed. A third had a film star's face on it.

"There's a fact card here," Dev said, reading off the display. "In March 1933, Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda." He said the word "propaganda" out loud, then said it again, slower, like it tasted strange.

Austin stared at the crowd poster. Everyone marching together, no one asking why. Glowing words stacked against plain ones. A famous face doing the convincing. He pulled out his phone and opened the chat, scrolling up through two hundred Vortex messages with new eyes. It wasn't random at all. It was the same moves, just selling a drink instead of a government.

At lunch he ran a test. He posted, "Vortex Fuel is the official drink of people who can't think for themselves," and waited. The replies split. Half the guys kept chanting "everyone's switching." But three of them stopped, went quiet, and one, Priya's brother Sam, sent a private message: "Okay, that poster thing got to me too. I only wanted it because everyone else did."

Austin wrote back, "Same. I almost begged my mom for five dollars last night." He told Sam he'd felt that pull without knowing where it came from, and Sam confessed he'd already bought two cans, both untouched in his locker. After school they traded screenshots of the wildest messages, sorting them into piles: bandwagon, loaded words, celebrity. "Eleven of these just say 'everyone,'" Sam said. "Nine use the word 'weak' for people who don't drink it."

Mrs. Okafor walked past their bench and glanced at the screen. "Homework or mischief?" she asked. Austin held up the phone so she could see the sorted list. She read it, nodded once, and kept walking. Sam typed one more message into the main chat, short and plain: "Drink whatever you want. Just count the tricks first." Below it, Dev replied with a single eye-roll emoji, and then, a minute later, a photo of himself drinking water.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Glittering generalities are vague, positive words like "freedom" or "natural" that make people feel good about something without saying anything specific or checkable.
story:
Layla had forty dollars and one hour before her mom picked her up at the food court. She wanted the Starlet sneakers, the purple ones with the silver stripe, and she had seen them the second she walked past the shoe store window. Inside, a screen above the shelves played the same commercial over and over: the rapper Dez Flow sprinting down a hallway in the sneakers, saying they were the only shoe he trusted. Two girls beside Layla pointed at the screen. "Everybody at school has these," one said. "You're literally the last person."

The price tag read seventy-five dollars. Layla counted her money again in her pocket. Forty. She could speculate about asking her mom for the rest, but her mom would ask why she needed them, and the honest answer was that everyone had them and Dez Flow said they were great, which even Layla could hear was not much of a reason.

She drifted toward the grocery aisle of the mall's big drugstore, where her little brother Omar was supposed to be picking a cereal with the ten dollars their mom had given him. He stood holding a box with a red banner that shouted ALL-NATURAL GOODNESS across the top. "This one," he said. "It's natural. That means it's good for you." Layla took the box from him and turned it over. The ingredient list ran eleven lines long, and the third word was sugar, followed later by three other syrups. "Natural" was on the front but nowhere on the back, and nothing on the box said what "goodness" meant or how anyone could check it.

"Where'd you learn to do that?" Omar asked. "Mom's hygiene teacher thing," Layla said. "She had a poster. Vague, positive words like natural or freedom that just make you feel good without saying anything specific. Glittering generalities." Omar frowned at the box. "So the front is basically lying." "Not lying," Layla said. "Just not saying anything." She looked at the boxes on either side: PROVEN TRUST, PURE ENERGY, REAL QUALITY. Every one of them sounded strong and meant nothing she could test. She realized the shoe ad had done the same thing. Dez Flow trusted the shoes. Trusted them to do what, exactly? He never said.

Omar put the red box back and picked one whose ingredient list started with whole grain oats and had six lines total. Then he tugged her sleeve. "You still want the purple ones." "Everyone has them," Layla said, and heard herself. The store's own speaker was playing a jingle with the words "Join the movement," which was the same trick in a different hat.

She walked back to the shoe store and found a plain pair, purple without the silver stripe, on the clearance rack for thirty-eight dollars. She tried them on, walked a circle, and paid. Outside the store she sat on a bench, laced them tight, and put her old shoes in the box.

When Omar arrived with his cereal, he pointed at her feet. "Those aren't the ones everybody has." "Nope," Layla said, and stood up. "Race you to the food court."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: 2 is the only even prime number, because every larger even number can be divided evenly by 2.
story:
Payton sat at Grandpa's kitchen table with his old laptop open in front of her, the screen showing the little program she had typed. It asked for a number, then checked every number from 2 up to the one you entered, looking for a divisor. If it found none, it printed "prime." She needed it to work by Sunday, because her computer club was having a showcase and she had promised Ms. Ruiz a demo. Grandpa slurped his coffee behind her, unhelpful and cheerful about it.

She typed 9 and got "not prime," which was right. She typed 7 and got "prime," also right. Then she typed 2, and the screen said "not prime." Payton frowned and leaned closer, as if the answer might change if she stared hard enough. The kitchen smelled like burnt toast from Grandpa's third attempt at breakfast.

"That's wrong," she said. "Two has to be prime." She traced the loop in her mind, the invisible path the program took. Start at 2, divide the input by 2, then 3, then upward. With an input of 2, the first number it tried was 2 itself, and 2 divided by 2 left nothing over, so her code said "not prime." The bug was hidden inside the loop, where she couldn't see it, but she could see its footprint on the screen.

She tried an idea: stop the loop before it reaches the number itself, so the program only tests divisors smaller than the input. She exhale'd slowly through her nose, changed one character, and ran it again. Two came back "prime." She pumped her fist, and Grandpa raised his coffee mug like a diplomat sealing a treaty, which is what he called it whenever she and the computer reached an agreement.

Then she tried 4, and it said "not prime," and 6, and 8, and 10, all "not prime," every single one. Payton sat back and looked at the pattern building up in her notebook, a cumulative list of results running down the page. "Every even number after 2 fails," she said slowly. "Because they can all be divided evenly by 2." Two was the only even prime there was. Her whole notebook suddenly made sense, prime down one column, not prime down the other, and the evens sat stubbornly on the wrong side except for that one lonely 2 at the top.

She wrote a comment in the code so she would remember, then added one more line so the program would say something special when someone entered 2. Grandpa leaned over her shoulder, toast in hand. "Try yours truly's favorite number," he said. She typed in 2 and hit enter, and the screen glowed back at them: "Prime. The only even one."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Baking powder already contains both baking soda and a dry acid, so it can make batter rise without an acidic ingredient in the recipe.
story:
Ethan had budgeted his Saturday down to the minute: two hours at the community kitchen to bake biscuits for tonight's family dinner, because Mom had picked up an extra shift and there was no money for takeout this week. The kitchen smelled like the bread Mr. Alvarez had left cooling on the rack, and Ethan spread his flour, butter, and the recipe card Mom had written out in her slanted handwriting. Everything was going fine until he opened the tin marked BAKING POWDER and found it empty, except for a few pale dustings on the bottom.

He stared into the tin as if more powder might appear. Under the counter, though, sat a box of baking soda, and on the side of it, in cheerful letters, were the words "bakes up light and fluffy." Close enough, he decided, and measured out exactly what the recipe asked for.

That was his first mistake, though he didn't know it yet.

While he cut the butter into the flour, his friend Dani arrived, dragging her little brother Marcus, who wanted, more than anything in the world, to be allowed to crack an egg. "One egg," Marcus said. "I've cracked an egg at home. Twice." Ethan had seen the results of one of those attempts, a biscuit bowl full of shell fragments, so he handed Marcus a spoon and the job of stirring the milk, which Marcus accepted with the expression of someone being asked to scrub floors.

The dough went into the oven, and Ethan washed up, pleased with himself. It was Dani, peering at the recipe card, who frowned. "Why does it say baking powder here, if you used soda?" Ethan shrugged. "Same thing, basically." She didn't look convinced, and the more he thought about it, the less convinced he got. He remembered last month, when Mom made buttermilk pancakes and reached for the soda box on purpose. Buttermilk. That was tangy. His biscuit recipe had nothing tangy in it at all, just flour, butter, milk, salt, and the powder in question. Something wasn't matching up.

He found Mrs. Okoye, who ran the kitchen on Saturdays, restocking the spice shelf, and asked her point blank. "Baking powder already contains both baking soda and a dry acid," she said, "so it can make batter rise without an acidic ingredient in the recipe." She said it like she was reading a grocery list, then went back to her shelf, leaving Ethan standing there with the whole problem suddenly clear. His soda had no partner. It was sitting in the oven with nothing to react with, as useless as Marcus's spoon.

The biscuits came out flat and dense, like pale hockey pucks. Marcus bit one anyway and announced, "Tastes like glue," which was harsh but not entirely wrong. Ethan refused to be defeated by an obstinate biscuit. He checked the fridge, found a carton of buttermilk someone had donated, and started over, this time swapping the regular milk for buttermilk so the soda would have something to work with. The second batch rose golden and tall, and when he pulled them out, Marcus grabbed the biggest one and held it up like a trophy. "I stirred that," he said.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Homesickness is the distress of being away from home and familiar people; it is common after a move and usually eases as a person settles in.
story:
The moving truck rattled over a seam in the highway, and Madison's box of keepsakes slid an inch toward the back door. She was riding between her mother and a lamp shaped like a flamingo, because the family car had been sold two weeks early and there had been no other seat. Through the gap in the rolled-down door she watched telephone poles flick past like fence pickets, counting them to keep her mind off the last thing her best friend Priya had said: "You'll forget us by Christmas."

At a rest stop, Madison dug through the keepsake box until she found the photograph of Maple Street, all six kids from number 14 through 22 lined up on the curb after the snowball battle of last February. She held it up to the truck's open door so the light could reach it, and to her annoyance her eyes stung and a tear dropped right onto Priya's snow boot. She wiped it with her sleeve and frowned at herself. She was not hurt. Nobody had died. She had simply woken up that morning in a motel with a ceiling she didn't recognize, and the strange ceiling had followed her all day like a shadow.

"Traffic's consistent on this route," her mother said, climbing back into the cab with two bottles of juice. "Stop and go, stop and go." Madison didn't answer. She was thinking about something else, a pattern she was trying to pin down. Her grandmother had cried at the airport when she flew back to Tucson last summer, and by the time she video-called in September she had been laughing about her tomato plants. Her cousin Dev had refused to eat for two days at sleepaway camp, and by day ten he'd been the one leading songs at the bonfire. It was as if the sadness of leaving wasn't about the place itself. It was about being away from familiar people, and it seemed to have a shape, a beginning and a middle and, if you waited, an end.

"It's called homesickness," her mother said quietly, noticing the photograph still in Madison's hand. "It's what being away from home does to you. Almost everybody gets it after a move." Madison nodded and slid the picture back into the box, but she didn't put the lid on. She had a theory forming, and she intended to test it the way she tested things: by collecting evidence.

The evidence would have to come from the new town. They arrived on a Thursday, and the new house smelled like paint and strangers. On Friday Madison sat on her unmade bed and felt the ceiling pressing down, unfamiliar and gray, and she wrote in her notebook: Day One, terrible. On Saturday she met the girl across the street, a tall kid named Rosa who was trying to teach her dog to catch a frisbee in the maple canopy overhead, tossing it low so it skimmed under the leaves. Rosa missed every throw, and the dog just sat down, and somehow this made Madison laugh until she had to lean on the fence.

"You laugh at everything or just at Badger?" Rosa asked.

"Just at dogs who don't catch things," Madison said, and realized she had gone a whole hour without thinking about Maple Street.

By the following week she had filled a page with her data. Day one, terrible. Day three, medium. Day five, she had eaten two helpings of noodles at Rosa's house while Rosa's brothers argued about which birds migrate farther, geese or Arctic terns, and Madison had said terns and been right. Day eight, she had waved at the mail carrier and known his name was Frank. The pattern held exactly the way her grandmother's and Dev's had. The sadness wasn't permanent; it drained away as the town filled up with familiar things, and familiar people, and ceilings she recognized. On day nine she taped the photograph of Maple Street to her wall, right next to a blurry new one of Rosa and Badger and the frisbee stuck in the maple branches.

That evening her phone buzzed. It was a message from Priya: a picture of the old curb, empty, with the caption "You there?" Madison typed back, "Here. You won't believe where this frisbee is stuck," and attached the photo.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: Portable generators and charcoal grills give off carbon monoxide, so safety agencies say to run them only outdoors, far from doors and windows, never in a house or garage.
story:
The lights went out at Grandma Ruth's farmhouse just as Isla was labeling her science diagram of a frog, its long curled intestine the last part she had left to name. The refrigerator hummed down into silence, and outside the window the whole valley went black except for a few stars. Grandma Ruth felt her way to the junk drawer and found two flashlights, and Grandpa pulled on his boots.

"Generator time," he said, and Isla followed him through the dark kitchen, her flashlight beam hopping across the floor. He opened the door to the garage and Isla heard him fumbling with the pull cord on the big portable generator he used after storms. It sat right there between the car and the workbench, and beside it, propped near the door to the kitchen, was an extension cord already coiled and ready.

"Grandpa, wait." She was hesitant at first, because he had run farms for forty years and she had only read a safety flyer at school last week. "That generator gives off carbon monoxide. You're only supposed to run it outdoors, far from doors and windows. Never in a house or a garage. That's what the flyer said, exactly."

Grandpa stood still with his hand on the cord. "Huh," he said. "My father ran his in the barn."

"Please?" Isla said. "We can run the cord under the garage door and set it way out past the porch."

Grandpa rubbed his chin, then he and Isla wrestled the heavy machine onto a dolly, rolled it down the driveway, and parked it far from the house, its exhaust pointing at the open field. Grandpa had to adjust the choke twice before it coughed to life, and when the lamps came back on inside, Grandma Ruth called from the porch that she was heating water for cocoa on the camp stove out on the steps, not in the kitchen, since she had read the same flyer.

The twist came when Mr. Alvarez from the next farm over trudged up the driveway with his own flashlight. "You folks got power from somewhere?" he asked. "My wife's on one of those breathing machines and the battery won't last the night." Isla remembered something then, a low rumbling she had heard through her window during last spring's storm, coming from the direction of the Alvarez place. "Mr. Alvarez," she asked, "when you run your generator, where do you put it?"

He blinked. "In the garage, with the door cracked."

Isla looked at Grandpa, and Grandpa looked at Mr. Alvarez. "Come on," Grandpa said, picking up the spare gas can. "We'll get yours set up outside, nice and far from your doors, and we'll run you a line."

They crunched off down the gravel together, three flashlights bobbing in the dark.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: In the United States, Feeding America is a nationwide network of more than 200 food banks.
story:
On Saturday morning Lucy stood in her own driveway, staring at a truck parked beside the garage, and felt a little intimidated by the crowd already forming down the sidewalk. Her mom had signed them up to host a mobile food pantry, which meant strangers would carry boxes of groceries through their yard all day. Lucy hadn't wanted this. She had wanted a quiet weekend, and she said so twice at breakfast, until her mom pointed out that Mrs. Okafor next door had asked for help and couldn't lift heavy boxes anymore.

"You can be in charge of the check-in table," her mom said, dragging two folding tables onto the lawn.

Lucy sorted cans and wrote tally marks, but something kept catching her eye. The first truck that arrived was from a food bank in their own city, and on its side was a blue logo with a bowl shape. An hour later a second truck rolled up, from two towns over, and it wore the exact same logo. Then a third, from a city an hour away. Same blue bowl. At first she thought it was an illusion, that she was seeing the design wrong, that no two different places would paint identical marks on their trucks.

She asked the driver of the third truck, a man with flour on his sleeves. "Why do all the trucks have that same picture?"

"That's the network," he said, hoisting a crate down. "It's called Feeding America. It's a nationwide network of more than 200 food banks."

"Two hundred," Lucy repeated, and thought about that while she worked. It explained the boxes, too. Every carton she opened had the same logo stamped on the corner, even though the trucks came from different cities. The rule she'd been guessing at wasn't a rule at all; it was a system, invisible until you noticed the same mark three times.

A boy her age, Marcus, showed up with his grandmother, who wanted oranges but couldn't see the crate at the far end of the table. He kept asking Lucy if there were any left, because his grandmother wouldn't eat the canned peaches, and he wanted to find her something fresh. Lucy had been about to say no, the oranges were gone, when she remembered the unopened crate still sitting in the garage. She carried it out, and Marcus's grandmother chose three, careful as a jeweler, and thanked Lucy twice.

"So this is okay?" her mom asked at the end of the afternoon, nodding at the emptied driveway, the folded tables, the neighbors walking home with bags.

Lucy looked at the last truck pulling away, blue bowl on its side, bound for some other city she'd never visit. "Can we do it again next month?"

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japan, bowing is a common greeting, and generally the longer and deeper the bow, the more respect it shows.
story:
Daniel had been dreading the party for a week, ever since his mother announced that Kenji's grandparents were flying in from Osaka and everyone was gathering at Aunt Rosa's house. Kenji had been Daniel's best friend since September, but Daniel had never met the grandparents, and he wanted badly to make a good impression. The problem was that he didn't know the rules. At his own family gatherings, you shook hands or hugged, you brought a plate of something, and you waited for Grandma to sit down before anyone ate. Kenji's family, he suspected, ran on a different program.

He stood on the porch holding a wrapped box of maple candy, which he had chosen himself, and listened to the doorbell chime. When the door opened, Kenji's grandfather bowed. It wasn't a little head nod like Daniel's uncle gave at church; the man bent from the waist, slowly, and held it. Daniel stuck out his hand at the same moment, so his hand floated in the air between them while the old man's face pointed at the floor. Kenji's grandmother bowed too, a smaller, quicker bow, and then they were both straight again, smiling, and Daniel's hand dropped to his side like a shot bird.

Inside, the folding tables had been pushed together into one long line that filled the whole living room. Kenji's grandmother presented Aunt Rosa with a bundle of cloth-wrapped packages, and Aunt Rosa hurried to the closet to dig out the gift she had hidden there, as if she had forgotten that giving went both ways. Daniel watched from the kitchen doorway and started counting. When the grandfather greeted Aunt Rosa, he bowed about fifteen degrees, brief and light. When he turned to greet Aunt Rosa's father, the oldest person in the room, the bow went deep and slow, almost to the table's edge, and stayed there long enough for Daniel to count to four. There it was, a pattern: the deeper and longer the bow, the more respect it carried. The fifteen-degree one was pocket change; the deep one was a gold coin.

Daniel had a plan to test before dinner. He waited until Grandfather Ota settled into a chair by the window, then walked over, held out the candy with both hands the way Kenji's grandmother had offered her packages, and bowed. He bent as far as his balance allowed and held it, counting silently, one, two, three, four. When he straightened, the old man's eyes were bright. He said something to Kenji, who laughed.

"He says you bow like a resilient young reed," Kenji translated. "Also, sit with your palms up, not on the table like a hammer. Grandmother hates that."

Daniel looked down at his hands, already flat on the table, and flipped them over. "Like this?"

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Día de los Muertos, celebrated in Mexico mainly on November 1 and 2, honors family members who have died with home altars called ofrendas.
story:
Gabriel's mother handed him a small framed photo the moment they reached the park gate. "Don't bend it," she said. "It's the only one of your abuela we have for today." The cultural center had set up tables under the pavilion, and Gabriel's class was helping build the altar for the Día de los Muertos celebration. He knew the holiday happened on the first and second of November, because his mother had circled both dates on the kitchen calendar, and he knew it was a way of honoring family members who had died. What he hadn't expected was that his own family would be part of it.

Mrs. Ruiz from the center gave them instructions. "We are building an ofrenda," she said, pointing to the wooden tiers. "That's what the altar is called." Gabriel watched Sofia from his class place a photo of her great-grandfather on the top tier, smoothing the frame with two fingers. His mother had told him the ofrenda was like the ones families made in their homes in Mexico, though his family had never made one before.

Then his cousin Mateo bumped him from behind, chasing a soccer ball, and Gabriel's hands were suddenly empty. The photo had gone. He knelt and swept his fingers through the grass. Nothing. The irony was sharp: the one object his mother had trusted him to carry, and he had lost it in the first five minutes.

He made himself stop and think instead of running in circles. The wind had picked up right when Mateo hit him. It came from the direction of the pond, steady and strong. A thin photo frame would slide on dry grass, and the ground sloped downhill toward the water. If he guessed right, the wind would have accelerated the frame along the slope, not across it. So the photo should be somewhere along a line between the pavilion and the pond, and the slope would make it drift faster and farther than it could have gone on flat ground.

He walked the line slowly, squinting. Leaves had blown into a drift against the base of an invasive bush, some kind of spiky plant with red berries that Mrs. Ruiz had complained about at the last cleanup, and there among the leaves was a corner of silver frame.

Gabriel lifted the photo out, checked the glass for cracks, and carried it back with both hands. He set it on the second tier, next to Sofia's great-grandfather. His mother came over from the food tables and looked at the altar for a long moment.

"There she is," she said. "Your abuela would have liked this. She always wanted us to do it properly, both days, not just one."

Sofia leaned over and straightened the frame so it faced the crowd. "Now we wait for tomorrow," she said.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: The forearm has two bones: the radius, on the thumb side, and the ulna, on the little-finger side.
story:
Alexa sat in the back seat with her new orange cast propped on a pillow, staring at the place where the doctor had taped a copy of her X-ray to the folder in her lap. Mom pulled out of the parking lot and pointed the car toward home. "You did great in there," Mom said. "The nurse said most kids cry when they set a bone."

"I did cry," Alexa said. "Just before the medicine." She turned the X-ray toward the window light. Two pale stripes ran down her forearm, side by side, and only one of them had a dark crack in it, like a hairline in a windshield. She couldn't tell which stripe was which, and that bothered her more than the ache did.

In her mind she replayed the doctor's voice while he pointed at the film. "The forearm has two bones," he had said. "The radius, on the thumb side, and the ulna, on the little-finger side." Alexa laid her good hand flat on her knee and copied it with the cast arm, slow and careful, the way she was being meticulous about every movement now. The crack in the X-ray sat closer to the thumb stripe. So the broken one should be the radius. But her thumb side barely hurt. The worst ache ran down by her little finger instead, and that didn't fit.

"Mom, can we stop at the pool office?" she asked. "I have to enroll for the swim team before Friday, or the spot goes to the next kid on the list." Mom glanced in the mirror. "You heard the doctor. Six weeks, no swimming." "He said no swimming with the cast," Alexa said. "He didn't say anything about being on the team. Priya said they let injured kids do the dryland drills, the stretching and the running, until they're cleared." She had built her whole plan on that premise, and she knew Mom would try to poke a hole in it.

She tested her idea in the seat, wiggling first her thumb, then her little finger. The thumb moved almost freely. The little finger sent a thin wire of pain up the outside of her arm, and she hissed through her teeth. That settled it. The cracked stripe in the picture wasn't the radius at all, because the doctors had turned the film around when they handed it to her; the image was flipped, like a mirror. It was the ulna that was broken, the little-finger bone, which explained exactly where it hurt. "Two minutes at the office," she told Mom. "I'll sign the form left-handed."

Mom sighed and put on the blinker. "Two minutes. And don't you dare take that pen out of the cast pocket with your teeth." Alexa grinned, tucked the X-ray folder under her good arm, and reached for the door handle before the car had fully stopped.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: A null hypothesis is the statement that there is no relationship between the things being studied, which an experiment then tries to reject.
story:
Megan's bean plants stood in two rows on the science fair table, and the ones that had spent three weeks next to the speaker looked exactly as sorry as the ones that had grown in silence. She had wanted this project to work so badly. First prize was a summer camp scholarship, and without it the camp would be out of reach, an expense her family could not manage twice.

Priya leaned over the pots, frowning. "So music doesn't help plants grow?"

"That's not what I can say yet," Megan said, turning her notebook around. Her data table showed heights for both groups, nearly identical. "Mr. Okafor said our whole write-up is wrong because we never decided what no effect would look like. We just hoped the music plants would be taller."

Priya picked up the notebook and read the red comment at the top of the page. "Define your null hypothesis before you test it." She looked up. "What's that?"

"It's the statement that there's no relationship between the things you're studying," Megan said. "Music and growth, for us. The experiment doesn't prove music helps. It tries to reject that statement."

Priya set the notebook down slowly. "So if we'd written it down first, the null would say the two groups grow the same."

"And then our data would either knock it down or not," Megan said. She pointed at the rows of numbers. "Right now they're so close that I can't reject it. The plants grew the same either way." She felt her throat tighten and kept talking anyway. "But that's still a result. Judges want to see how you decide, not just whether you win."

They rebuilt the display board right there between the volcano and the homemade lava lamp. Megan wrote the null hypothesis across the top in careful block letters, then drew the height chart beneath it with both groups' bars nearly even. A boy from the next table wandered over, saw the board, and asked whether music had helped. "Not that I can show," Megan told him. "They look about equal, so the null stands."

When the judge stopped at their table, she asked Priya what they would change. Priya said, "We'd decide in advance what difference would signify a real effect, so we wouldn't just be hoping."

The judge nodded and made a mark on her clipboard. "Resilient beans, too," she said, tapping a pot. "They survived three weeks of my daughter's playlist."

Megan laughed, and straightened the tallest plant in the silent row. "Round two next year," she said. "Quieter music, bigger pots."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Before most scientific papers are published in a journal, other experts in the field review them for errors, a process called peer review.
story:
Eleanor had exactly one weekend to finish her science project on water quality, and she had just found the most bizarre website of her life. It showed photographs of a green, murky pond turning crystal clear in three days, all because of a special powder sold by a man named Dale. "One scoop a week and your water worries are over," Dale wrote beneath a picture of himself holding a jar. Eleanor leaned closer to the screen, her cat Pixel hopping onto the desk beside the keyboard. Her teacher had said every claim in the project needed a reliable source, and this one seemed too good to be true.

She typed "Dale's Clear Water Powder" into the search box and found something unexpected: a real science journal article about pond water, written by three researchers. On the first page, in small print, the article said it had been reviewed by two other experts before publication. Eleanor had never noticed a line like that before. She scrolled back to Dale's site and read every word, but nowhere did it say anyone had checked his work. It was just his own story, one person's experience with his own pond.

At dinner she told her older brother, Marcus, about the difference. "The journal article says experts looked at it before it got published," she said. "It's called peer review." Marcus nodded between bites of pasta. "So Dale's site is just him talking," he said. "Nobody checked anything." Eleanor pushed her noodles around her plate, thinking. The consequence of trusting Dale could be a bad grade, or worse, a project full of nonsense.

She wanted to document the difference properly, so she set up her own small test in the kitchen. She filled two identical jars with cloudy water from the fish tank filter, added a pinch of ordinary baking soda to one and nothing to the other, and labeled them with masking tape. Then she took photographs each morning and wrote down what she saw. By Sunday, both jars looked almost the same, which told her something real: a single scoop of anything was not a magic fix, and one person's glowing story proved nothing.

On Monday she turned in her project with both sources side by side, explaining which one had been examined by experts and which had not, and what her own jar test showed. Her teacher wrote "Excellent comparing" at the top in green pen. That afternoon, Eleanor opened her laptop and, out of curiosity, checked Dale's site one more time. There was a new comment at the bottom of the page, from someone named Ponds4Life: "Tried it for a month, my water's still green." Eleanor grinned and closed the lid.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Chinese, the word for 'four' sounds very similar to the word for 'death', so some buildings in East Asia skip the fourth floor.
story:
Marcus had one job on Friday: bring a snack to share for the international foods lesson, and not embarrass himself in front of Wei's grandmother, who was visiting from Hong Kong and coming to watch. He had brought a box of grape juice and a bag of pretzels. It felt thin.

When Wei invited him over Thursday evening to practice, Marcus said yes mostly because Wei's building had the fastest elevator in town. They rode up together, and Marcus pressed the button for Wei's floor. That was when he noticed the panel. The buttons went one, two, three, five. He counted them twice, dragging his finger along the row to be sure.

"Your building doesn't have a four," he said. "That's not a mistake? Buildings don't just skip numbers."

Wei looked at the panel like he was meeting an old acquaintance. "My grandma says in Chinese, the word for four sounds like the word for death," he said. "So some buildings in East Asia skip the fourth floor." Then he shrugged, as if floors were only floors, and the doors opened.

Marcus tested the idea in his head on the way down. If the number were bad luck, it would be missing in other buildings too. In his own building, the fourth floor was right where it should be, home to Mrs. Okafor and her parrots. So it wasn't a law of nature. It was a custom, the way his own family hugged hello and Wei's family bowed slightly, palms together, which Wei had demonstrated that morning with the gravity of a chess move.

At the lesson, Wei's grandmother brought egg tarts in a tin, and Wei passed them out with both hands, which Marcus copied and nearly dropped doing. When he handed one back to say thank you for a second tart, she waved it off and pressed it toward him again, and it took him three tries to understand that refusing once was polite and accepting twice was the point. The whole class ended up eating with their hands or with chopsticks or, in Marcus's case, with a pretzel used as tongs, which even he had to admit was not thriving.

After school, Marcus walked home the long way, parallel to the creek, and thought about how his street had houses from a hundred years ago, one of the oldest settlements in town, and how nobody could see that just by looking. Customs were like that. Hidden floors in an elevator you hadn't ridden yet.

He stopped at the corner store and bought a box of mooncakes, which the label said were red bean. He would bring them Monday, with both hands.

"Mrs. Okafor is on four," he told his dad at dinner. "Of a building with no four in it."

His dad blinked twice. "I'm going to need you to start from the beginning."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Countries that use metres write normal vision as 6/6 instead of 20/20; both describe the same eyesight.
story:
Gabriella sat on the spinning stool at Bright Eyes Optical and swung her legs, waiting for her new glasses to be made. Her mother was filling out forms at the counter, which meant Gabriella had time to text her cousin Dev, who had just moved from London.

"How did your eye test go?" she typed.

"Perfect," Dev wrote back. "The doctor says I have 6/6 vision."

Gabriella stared at the screen. Six out of six? That sounded like a grade, and not a good one. If 20/20 was perfect, then 6/6 had to be way down the chart, like getting a six on a twenty-point quiz. She typed, "Only 6?? I'm getting glasses because my eyes are 20 something. Are you okay?" Dev replied with a row of laughing faces, which was no help at all.

Fine. She would investigate. Gabriella spun her stool toward the exam room, where the optometrist was hanging a new eye chart, and stood in the doorway with her chin lifted in a way her mother called her ambassador face, the one she used when about to ask for something. "Excuse me," she said. "If someone has 6/6 vision, is that terrible?"

The optometrist laughed. "Where's this someone from?"

"London. England. He just moved."

"That'll do it. Countries that use metres write normal vision as 6/6 instead of 20/20. Same eyes, different measurement."

Gabriella did the math in her head, sort of. So 6/6 was not a failing grade; it was perfect vision wearing a different coat. Dev hadn't been bragging badly or hiding a disaster. He'd been bragging correctly. She felt her cheeks go warm, then decided to be defiant about it and blame the eye drops. She marched back to the waiting area and typed, "You have perfect vision, you smug show-off."

"Naturally," Dev wrote. "Are those glasses emojis supposed to be you?"

Before she could answer, the technician called her name and handed over the new glasses, purple frames with tiny stars on the hinges. Gabriella slid them on, and the whole store sharpened like someone had finally focused a camera. She could read the tiny price stickers on the lens cleaner. She could see that the poster of an eye near the ceiling had eyelashes, which seemed like showing off.

She walked to the counter, where her mother was signing the last form. "Mom, guess what. Dev sees six out of six, which is the same as my twenty out of twenty, except his is in metres."

"His what is in metres?"

"His vision. His perfect, annoying vision." Gabriella pushed the glasses up her nose. "Also, I've decided to enroll in optometry school so I can put those little letter charts on people's walls."

Her mother paid, shaking her head. Gabriella waved at the optometrist on the way out. "Six out of six!" she announced to the whole parking lot.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: The Rubin vase, introduced by Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin in 1915, can be seen as either a vase or two faces, but not both at the same moment.
story:
At dinner, Charlotte's little brother slammed his fork down and pointed at her. "The poster at the community center is two faces," he insisted. "Two faces looking at each other. I saw it today."

"It is a vase," said her mother, ladling soup into bowls. "A white vase on a black background. I walk past it every Tuesday."

Charlotte stopped with her spoon halfway to her mouth. That was strange. Her mother and Dex had looked at the exact same poster, in the exact same hallway, and they had come home with completely different pictures in their heads. "Can you both see the other thing?" she asked. "Mom, can you see the faces? Dex, can you see the vase?"

Dex squinted at the ceiling as if the poster were painted up there. "Sort of? If I try really hard. But then the vase goes away."

"It's like a treaty," their mother said, smiling. "You can only have one at a time."

Charlotte pushed her bread around her plate, thinking. After dinner she found the community center's website and searched for the poster. There it was: black and white, and once she knew what to look for, she could make the white part pop out as a vase, or let the black part take over and become two faces in profile, nose to nose. It flipped. She made it flip again. But no matter how hard she tried, she could not hold both pictures at once, the way you could look at a picture of a dog and a cat together. It was vase, or it was faces. Never both.

Underneath the image she found a caption. "This is called a Rubin vase," she read aloud, and Dex leaned over her shoulder. It said the Rubin vase was introduced by a Danish psychologist named Edgar Rubin in 1915, and that it could be seen as either a vase or two faces, but not both at the same moment.

"So Mom was right," said Dex.

"So you were both right," said Charlotte. "That's the weird part." She was skeptical of one thing, though. Maybe it only worked because they expected it to. Tomorrow at school she would nominate the poster for show-and-tell, draw it big on paper, and ask her class to call out what they saw without any hints. If kids who had never heard of it still saw only one picture at a time, then it wasn't just her family being strange. It was something about how seeing itself worked, some hidden rule in the brain you couldn't watch directly, only test from the outside, like guessing what was inside a wrapped present by shaking it.

The next afternoon she stood at the whiteboard with her marker squeaking, filling in the black around the white vase shape. "First person to raise a hand," she said, capping the marker, "tell me what you see."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Using separate cutting boards for raw meat and for ready-to-eat foods like salad prevents cross-contamination, the spread of bacteria from one food to another.
story:
The rain had finally stopped, though the sky outside the kitchen window still looked ominous, and Eleanor stood at the counter with a package of chicken thighs and a head of lettuce, determined to make dinner before Mom got home. Dad had said he would handle the ride to pick up her little brother, so the meal was hers alone. She wanted it to be good, not just edible, and she had even planned to elaborate on the usual Tuesday menu by adding a salad and garlic bread instead of plain rice.

She rinsed the chicken, patted it dry, and chopped it into strips on the big wooden cutting board. Then she slid the pieces into the pan, where they sizzled and popped, and turned to the lettuce. She was about to tear off the outer leaves and start chopping when she paused. The board in front of her still had faint smears from the raw chicken, and the knife lay beside it, damp from the meat.

Something tickled at the back of her mind, a memory of a poster in the cafeteria about keeping foods separate. She looked at the board, then at the lettuce, which nobody would cook. The chicken would spend ten minutes in a hot pan, but the salad would go straight from board to bowl to mouths. If the raw chicken had left something behind on the wood, it would ride the lettuce straight to the table. She could not see anything wrong. The board looked almost clean. But whatever the poster had been about, it was clearly about things you could not see.

Eleanor pulled open the drawer beneath the counter and found the green plastic board, the one Mom used for bread. She washed her hands, took a clean knife from the rack, and set up a whole separate station by the sink. "Separate boards," she said to herself. "Raw meat on one, ready-to-eat stuff on the other, so nothing spreads over."

Her neighbor Tomas appeared at the back door, drawn by the smell of garlic, and watched her juggle two boards. "Why not just use the one?" he asked.

"Raw chicken, then salad on the same board," Eleanor said. "That's cross-contamination."

"Sounds like a science project," Tomas said, and stole a piece of cucumber.

By the time the headlights swept the driveway, the chicken was golden, the salad was crisp in its blue bowl, and the two boards were drying on opposite sides of the sink. Mom came in with wet boots, sniffed the air, and dropped her bag on the chair. "You made all this?"

Eleanor slid the salad to the middle of the table. "Sit down before it gets soggy."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: According to the U.S. CDC, people with the flu are most contagious during the first three days of their illness.
story:
