Justin sat on the bench beside the pharmacy counter, sniffling into a tissue that had gone soft as an old sock. He was on day two of the flu, and although his fever had finally packed its bags, his nose had not. His mother stood at the window waiting for his prescription while the pharmacist typed with the speed of someone defrosting a freezer.

"I'm going to Dev's party on Friday," Justin announced, mostly to the ceiling.

"You're going nowhere," his mother said without turning around.

An old man in a plaid jacket who was also waiting looked over. "Big party?"

"Backyard, fourteen people, a taco bar," Justin said. "I'm the only one bringing hot sauce. It's a big responsibility."

The pharmacist slid a white bag across the counter. "Prescription for Marsh," she said, then, glancing at Justin's red nose, added, "Flu? Then listen, kid. You're most contagious during the first three days of your illness. After that it drops off." She rang up the old man's cough drops and moved on, as if she hadn't just handed Justin a mystery.

He did the math right there on the pharmacy bench, tapping his finger against his knee. Today was Tuesday, day two. Wednesday would be day three, Thursday day four, and Friday would be day five. The germs were like unwanted houseguests who only trashed the place for three days and then got bored. But if he sneezed on the taco bar on Friday, that would be fine. If he sneezed on it Wednesday, half of seventh grade would be home by the weekend. His original plan, going to the party early to prove he was fine, suddenly seemed like a terrible idea.

He tested his reasoning on the walk home, carrying the prescription bag like evidence. "So Wednesday's the danger day," he said to his mother. "Friday I'm practically harmless."

"That's not what the pharmacist said," his mother replied, "but I'll admit it's closer to the truth than your last argument."

Justin texted Dev from the couch, wrapped in the blanket where viruses clearly failed to thrive because he was already improving. He proposed moving the taco bar from Wednesday to Friday, citing the pharmacist like a lawyer citing a witness. Dev replied with a single thumbs-up and the message "my mom says yes, she says you're the only kid who ever researched a party."

The twist came Thursday, when Dev texted again: taco bar postponed, he had the flu now. Justin laughed so hard he started coughing, then called him. "What day are you on?"

"Day one," Dev groaned. "Why?"

Justin grinned at the ceiling. "You've got three days of being a walking sneeze. Mark your calendar. And save me a spot at the taco bar on day five."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In a 1974 study by Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, people who were asked how fast cars 'smashed' into each other gave higher speed estimates than people asked about cars that 'hit.'
story:
Maria raised her hand so fast her chair squeaked, and Mr. Doran still didn't call on her. He was busy writing "INTERPRETATION" on the board, which was the topic she wanted to argue about, because the topic was the reason she was in trouble at home.

It had started yesterday in the hallway. Her little brother, Theo, had come home from school and announced, "Dad asked me how fast you smashed into that kid by the lockers." Maria had barely brushed past a boy named Dev; her shoulder had touched his backpack and his water bottle had fallen. Yet Theo described her "running him over," and now she was grounded for the weekend, which meant missing the pool party, unless she could change her father's mind by dinner tonight.

"Here's your exit question," Mr. Doran said, checking the clock. "Ten minutes. Everyone saw the same video of the car accident on Monday. So why did half of you say the cars were going forty and half said twenty?"

Nobody answered. Maria looked around. Same video, same room, same morning. That made no sense to her, and things that made no sense bothered her the way a splinter bothered her thumb.

"Can I ask the class something?" she said. When Mr. Doran nodded, she stood up. "When I asked you to write your estimate, did anybody say the word smashed to you? Like, did I say, how fast did they smash into each other?"

Priya frowned at her paper. "You said smashed to our row. It was on my slip."

"It was on your slips?" Mr. Doran turned around, and Maria's ears went hot, because she hadn't planned to confess. But the clock gave her seven minutes, so she went on. "I handed out two versions. Half the slips said smashed and half said hit. I wanted to see if it mattered. It's for my dad. He thinks I did something I didn't."

"It mattered," said Priya, flipping through her notes. "We said forty and fifty. That's so sinister, actually. Just one word."

Marcus, whose slip had said hit, held up his paper. "I said twenty." Three other kids near him nodded.

Mr. Doran pulled a book off the shelf and set it on Maria's desk, open to a page. "Read the third paragraph out loud. Quietly, just to yourself." She read it twice. In 1974, two researchers, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, had asked people how fast cars smashed into each other, and those people gave higher speed estimates than people asked how fast cars hit. Same films, different word. She looked up, and Mr. Doran was already collecting the exit questions, because there were two minutes left.

At dinner she laid the book on the table, open to the page. "Dad, what exact words did you use when you asked Theo about the hallway?" Her father paused with his fork in the air. "I asked how fast Maria smashed into that kid. It was just a question."

"That's what the researchers found," Maria said. "One word, and the speed goes up. Dev dropped a bottle, Dad. Ask him. I'll install a tracking app on my phone if you don't believe me, but call his mom tonight."

Her father picked up his phone and dialed. Maria waited, watching Theo push peas around his plate, while the word extinction ran through her head, the way her science teacher used it, the dying out of a thing that used to exist. Maybe her bad reputation could go extinct too.

Her father hung up and set the phone down next to the open book. "Dev's mother says it was nothing. You're ungrounded." He looked at Theo. "And tomorrow I'm asking you different questions."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: When the price of one good rises, many buyers switch to a substitute, a similar good that does the same job, so demand for the substitute goes up.
story:
The line outside the Riverside Pavilion stretched past the bakery and around the corner, and Raphael had been standing in it since six in the morning. Ahead of him, a man in a gray jacket moved down the queue, saying the same words to every group he passed. "Box office tickets, eighty apiece. Limited number. Cash only."

Raphael counted his money again. Fifty-two dollars, saved from mowing lawms all June. The box office price was supposed to be forty, but the sign taped to the window that morning had changed things: "Limited tickets available." When he'd bought tickets for this same band last year, the line had been short and the seats had sat empty in whole rows.

"Eighty," the man in gray said again, closer now. "Going fast."

Behind Raphael, two girls were whispering. "My mom did this with chips last month," one of them said. "Her favorite brand jumped to six dollars a bag, so she just bought the store brand instead. It does the same job, basically. She calls it a substitute." Her friend laughed. "Your mom and her economics." Raphael turned the word over in his mind. Substitute. A similar thing that does the same job.

He looked down the street. Three blocks away, a smaller theater had put up a banner that morning: a tribute band, same songs, same night, tickets fifteen dollars, and the sign under the window read "Plenty of seats available." The line there had only eleven people in it. As he watched, a boy from the concert queue peeled off and walked toward it. Then a couple followed. Then a family of four. It was contagious, the way the little line began to grow while the big one barely shrank.

Raphael's heart pounded. If he stayed, the man in gray might sell out before he reached the window, and he'd have nothing. If he left, he'd see the songs performed, but not the real band. He made himself wait ten more minutes, watching, testing his idea. The concert line stayed long and hungry. The tribute line kept growing. When the man in gray shouted "Last four tickets, eighty each," four hands shot up at the front, and that settled it.

He walked the three blocks, bought a ticket for fifteen, and still had thirty-seven dollars left. Ahead of him in the new line, the two girls from the concert queue had appeared, and the one who'd talked about chips grinned at him. "You switched too?"

"Substitute," Raphael said, holding up his ticket.

The doors opened, and the line surged forward.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Delayed muscle soreness is not caused by lactic acid, which returns to normal levels within about an hour after exercise.
story:
The morning after Tuesday's practice, Simon's legs ached so much that walking down the bleacher steps felt like stepping onto two bricks. Marco, who caught for the team, climbed up beside him rubbing his shoulder.

"It's all that lactic acid," Marco said. "It builds up when we work hard."

Simon thought about that while they took infield drills. Practice had ended at five o'clock yesterday. His legs had felt fine at dinner, fine at bedtime, fine when he brushed his teeth this morning. The soreness had shown up today, more than a day later. If something was building up during practice, it seemed like it should hurt right after practice, not the next morning. He decided to run a test on himself. At the end of warmups he did ten full sprints from foul pole to foul pole, harder than he ever worked in a game, and then he waited.

An hour after the sprints, sitting in the dugout with his glove on his knee, he flexed his calves. Nothing hurt. He could feel his pulse in them, and they were warm, but the soreness was not there yet. The next morning it arrived, right on schedule, in both legs at once. It was the same pattern as Tuesday. Whatever was making his muscles sore, it was not still sitting in his legs from the exercise, because an hour after he stopped, everything felt normal. On Thursday he found Marco by the equipment shed, pumping up a flat football that someone had left in the bin. The pump handle squeaked with every stroke, and the ball grew round and firm with each push of air.

"Marco, I checked," Simon said. "I did sprints yesterday and felt fine an hour later. If lactic acid were the problem, it would have to stick around a whole day to make me sore this morning. It doesn't. It goes back to normal levels within about an hour after you exercise."

Marco stopped pumping and squinted at him. "Then what's making my shoulder hurt?"

"I don't know yet. But it isn't that."

Coach Alvarez walked past and told them practice was starting, and whether Marco's throw to second was late or on time, that was her call, though Marco muttered that the whole strike zone was subjective anyway, so why bother arguing. The football, fat with air now, sat on the bench forgotten. Simon picked it up, tossed it once in his hand, and handed it back to Marco.

"Hold onto this," he said. "We're testing your shoulder next."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Practicing in several shorter sessions spread over days usually builds a skill better than the same total time crammed into one long session.
story:
The trumpet felt like a brick in Anthony's hands, and Mr. Ruiz had already called his name twice. "Measure sixteen, Anthony. From the top." The music classroom smelled like valve oil and old carpet, and the radiators radiated a dry heat that made his fingers stiff. Anthony lifted the horn, blew, and cracked the same high note he had cracked every Tuesday for three weeks.

Beside him, Priya slid her flute onto her lap and leaned over. "You practice, right?" she whispered. "Sunday night? Because you sound great for the first eight measures and then it all falls apart."

"Two hours," Anthony admitted. "Last night. The whole book." He had meant it as proof. Priya's eyebrows went up, and something about her face made him feel like he'd said the wrong thing even though he'd done more work than she had.

At lunch, Anthony sat with his sandwich untouched and thought it through like a math problem. Priya practiced every single day, he knew that, because she'd told the whole section once. Maybe twenty minutes a day. He did two hours in one night. Two hours was six times twenty minutes, so his total time was way more than hers, and yet she played the solo and he cracked notes. Same amount of practice should mean same result. Unless the total wasn't the thing that mattered. Unless the spreading out was the thing. He turned his milk carton around and around. There was only one way to find out.

He made a chart on the back of his science folder and ruled it into small boxes: fifteen minutes before school, ten at night, every day until the next Tuesday. He didn't tell Priya, in case it didn't work. His little sister, Rosa, pounded the piano keys while he practiced, so he started leaving a bag of pretzels on the bench for her, and she settled into playing her own made-up songs at a gentler volume, which helped them both.

The first few days felt slow. He kept missing the same leap in measure sixteen, and his grandfather's old trumpet, a dented brass alloy that had survived two wars and one fall down a staircase, seemed to laugh at him. But on Thursday something odd happened. He picked up the horn, cold, no warm-up except a few long tones, and his fingers found the fingering for the high note before his brain did. He hadn't drilled it harder. He had just... come back to it, again and again, letting each short session do a little work while he slept, ate, walked to school.

On Tuesday, Mr. Ruiz raised his baton. "Measure sixteen. Anthony." The room went quiet. Priya gave him a tiny nod across the stand. Anthony took a breath, thought of nothing at all, and let his fingers go where they had learned to go. The high note came out round and silver, and the kid on trombone, who had declared trumpets obsolete ever since the school bought the low brass section new instruments, said, "Whoa," into his slide.

After class Priya caught him at the door. "So what changed?"

Anthony held up his folder, the chart with its rows of small checkmarks. "Same twenty minutes every day," he said. "Not two hours the night before. Turns out that's the whole trick." Priya grabbed a marker from her pocket and said, "Draw me one."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it.
story:
The photo went up at 9:02 on a Tuesday night: Willow doing her weird victory dance after finishing her science project, socks half off, face scrunched like a raisin. She had meant to send it only to Priya, but her thumb hit the whole group chat instead. Eighteen people. She deleted it within ten minutes, heart hammering, and then sat very still in her dark bedroom, watching the chat scroll on about weekend plans as if nothing had happened. She let herself breathe. Gone meant gone, she decided, and went to sleep.

At lunch the next day, Priya slid her phone across the table. "Look at this." In a different group chat, one Willow wasn't even in, someone had posted the photo with the caption "found this gem." Beneath it, people she barely knew were typing laughing faces and the word "iconic." Willow's stomach dropped. She had deleted it. How could it be here, in a place she couldn't reach?

"I don't get it," she said. "I took it down."

Priya shrugged. "Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot still has it."

Willow stared at the screen. So that was the rule. It wasn't magic; it was a copy, sitting in someone's camera roll, free to travel anywhere. She scrolled up and found the name of the account that had posted it: a boy named Marcus from her math class. She barely knew him. But the photo hadn't appeared out of nowhere, and somebody had to have passed it along.

That night she ran a test, the way she would for a lab. She posted a harmless picture of her cat to the group chat, waited exactly ten minutes, deleted it, and then texted Priya: "Did you screenshot it before it vanished?" Priya sent back a screenshot, timestamp and all, plus a smug message about how the cat deserved a citation for cuteness. Willow laughed, but her mind was working. The copy survived deletion. That was the whole answer. She couldn't unsend the dance photo, and envying people whose embarrassing moments never surfaced wouldn't help either. What she could do was be objective about the situation, like her science teacher kept saying: state the facts, then act.

The next morning she walked straight to Marcus's table in the cafeteria. "You posted my photo in the other chat," she said, keeping her voice level. "I'm not mad, but I want to know who sent it to you, because I deleted it and it still got around." Marcus looked uncomfortable, then held up his phone. "It was Priya. She thought it was hilarious. She said you'd figure it out eventually." Willow turned around. Priya was standing behind her, grinning, phone raised, and Willow's cat was already on the screen.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A tomato is botanically a fruit, but in 1893 the US Supreme Court ruled in Nix v. Hedden that it counted as a vegetable for import taxes.
story:
Riley pressed three tomato seeds into the dark soil of her aunt's farm and patted them down like she was tucking them into bed. She had claimed the plot behind the barn on day one, and by June the seedlings were knee-high, and by July she had green marbles swelling on every branch. Her plan was simple and enormous: sell her tomatoes at the farm stand by the road, next to her aunt's jam and eggs.

The trouble started at the stand on Saturday. A man in a sun hat picked up one of Riley's ripe red tomatoes, weighed it in his palm, and said, "You've got these in the wrong bin, kid. Tomatoes are fruit. They belong with the peaches."

"They're vegetables," Riley said. "They go in the salad, not the fruit bowl."

"Fruit," the man insisted. "Seeds on the inside. That's a fruit."

Riley's cousin Marisol leaned over the cash box. "Then cucumbers are fruit too. And peppers. And pumpkins."

The man laughed. "Pumpkins? Now you're being ridiculous."

Riley wanted to win this. More than that, she wanted to be right, which she had learned was not always the same thing. That night she borrowed her aunt's laptop and typed one question: is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable. The answer made her sit up straight. Botanically, a tomato was a fruit, full stop. But in 1893, the US Supreme Court had ruled in a case called Nix v. Hedden that for import taxes, tomatoes counted as vegetables. She read it twice, then read it to Marisol over the phone.

"Nix v. Hedden," Marisol repeated slowly, like she was chewing it. "So the Court decided taxes, not lunch."

"So both of us were right," Riley said, "and both of us were wrong. Wait till Sun Hat Man hears this."

Sunday morning, Riley made two signs on cardboard, testing her idea before anyone could argue. One read FRUIT, SCIENTIFICALLY SPEAKING. The other read VEGETABLE, ACCORDING TO THE SUPREME COURT. She set them on either side of the tomato bin with an arrow pointing between them. Her aunt walked by, paused, and said, "Very sophisticated display. Now wash your hands, stand hygiene, customers are watching you handle their food."

The man in the sun hat came back for more tomatoes. He read the signs, read them again, and rubbed his jaw. "Huh. I was scientifically right."

"And I was legally right," Riley said. "The Court said they could enforce the tax that way. So the vegetable side wins for money, and the fruit side wins for science."

He bought two pounds and told two other customers on his way out, loudly, that he had lost an argument to an eleven-year-old and enjoyed it. By noon the tomato bin was empty, and Marisol was drawing a third sign that said SOLD OUT, SCIENTIFICALLY AND LEGALLY. Riley ran back to the garden to count what was still ripening on the vines.

"Ten more turning red," she called. "Tell everyone to come back next Saturday."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed in the Great Vowel Shift after spellings had started to become fixed, which is a major reason English spelling often doesn't match pronunciation.
story:
The bleachers in the gymnasium smelled like floor wax and popcorn, and Victor sat on the front row of seats going over his word list one last time. He had lost the school bee last year on the word "bite," of all things, because in his head he spelled it the way it sounded and forgot the silent e. Ever since then, English spelling felt like a practical joke someone was playing on him.

Two nights before, he'd almost quit studying. He had thrown his pencil across the kitchen table and told his older sister, Dee, that English made no sense and he was going to postpone the whole thing until a language that made sense came along. Dee, who was frugal with sympathy, slid an old library book across the table instead of a speech. "Look at page forty," she said. So he did, and the page told him something he had never heard before. Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed in the Great Vowel Shift, and the shift happened after spellings had already started to become fixed. That, the book said, was a major reason English spelling often doesn't match pronunciation. Victor read the paragraph three times. The letters hadn't been lying all those years. People had just changed the way they said them, like a town that stays on the map after the frontier moves past it. He didn't suddenly like spelling, but he stopped feeling tricked by it, which turned out to matter more.

Now the principal stood at the microphone on the gym floor. "Contestant twelve, Victor Reyes." Victor walked out, his shoes squeaking on the varnish, and stood beside the judge's table.

"Your word is 'subtle.'"

Of course it was. A word with a silent b, sitting there like a taunt. Victor closed his eyes for a second and ran the pattern through his head: old spelling, shifted sound, the b had probably once done its job before the vowels moved on without it. It wasn't a guess anymore. It was the way the language was built.

"S-U-B-T-L-E," he said. "Subtle."

The judge checked her card and nodded. "Correct."

Victor grinned and walked back to his seat. On his way past the folding chairs he caught Dee's eye in the crowd and mouthed, "Great Vowel Shift." She gave him a thumbs up, and the principal cleared her throat for the next word.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Rotating crops, so the same plant family is not grown in the same spot year after year, helps keep soil pests and diseases from building up.
story:
Camille counted her coins twice at the Saturday farmers' market, because the tomato seedlings had to go in the ground before the end of the weekend, and she only had six dollars. "How much for two?" she asked the man at the plant table.

"Three dollars, but I have to warn you," he said. "These are the same variety your mom bought last year, and hers didn't do well."

"My tomatoes got brown spots and fell over," Camille said. "All of them. In the back corner, by the fence."

The man rubbed his chin. "You plant tomatoes in that corner every year?"

"Every year. It's the sunniest spot. What else would I put there?" She waited, but he only shrugged and handed her the seedlings, so she paid and carried them home, frowning.

That evening, she sat on the porch steps and thought about her grandmother's farm, which she visited two summers ago. She remembered walking between the long rows while her grandmother pointed. "Tomatoes here this year, beans here, cabbage there," her grandmother had said. "Next summer, they orbit around, each row takes a turn somewhere new." Camille had thought it sounded tedious, all that moving and mapping. Now she wondered why her grandmother bothered.

On Sunday morning, Camille knocked on Mrs. Petrov's door, because Mrs. Petrov had the best garden on the street. "Can I ask you something?" Camille said. "If somebody plants tomatoes in the same corner every year, and they start getting sick, is it the corner's fault?"

Mrs. Petrov set down her watering can. "It could be. My father rotated crops, always, so the same plant family was never grown in the same spot year after year. He said it keeps the soil from making trouble." She tilted her head. "You know what family tomatoes are in?"

"No."

"Same family as peppers. Not the same as beans, or carrots, or lettuce."

Camille walked home fast, carrying the idea like a full bucket. She dug up the wilted tomato stems from the corner and dropped them in the compost pile, where the decomposers would break them down into dark, crumbly soil over the winter. Then she planted her new seedlings in the middle bed, where the beans had grown last summer. It wasn't the sunniest spot, but she could see it from her window, and she marked the corner with a stick.

All through June she measured the plants with a ruler and drew a map of the yard in her notebook. In the top corner she wrote "tomatoes, last year, sick." In the middle bed she wrote "tomatoes, this year," and every week the number of green dots on her sketch grew. On the last day of school, she counted fourteen little hard green tomatoes hanging from healthy stems.

She ran inside to get her brother. "Come look," she said. "And next spring, the tomatoes move again."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A control group gets no change at all, giving a baseline to compare the tested groups against.
story:
Luca set the last cup on the folding table at the edge of the gymnasium, right under the banner that read Science Fair: Set Up by Noon. In front of him stood nine bean plants in paper cups, each one labeled with a sticky note. Three said Fertilizer A, three said Fertilizer B, and one just said Water. His best friend Marcus leaned over the table and squinted.

"Why does that one only get water?" Marcus asked. "That's like entering a race and not running."

"It's called a control group," Luca said. "It gets no change at all, so I can compare everything else against it."

The trouble was the control group was embarrassing him. Every other plant had grown at least a little, and his plain-water bean sat there with the same two sad leaves it had three weeks ago. Priya from his science class walked past, slowed down, and pointed.

"That one's dead, Luca."

"It's not dead, it's the baseline." He said it with more confidence than he felt. For weeks he had wondered whether his fertilizers were actually working. Fertilizer A plants were tall, B plants were medium, and the control was tiny. If he had no control, he would have nothing to measure against. Now he could see that A had grown twice as much as the plain-water plant, and B about half again as much. The tiny plant was doing its job by doing nothing.

Then Judge Okafor stopped at his table, and Luca's reputation as a kid who glued things together the night before felt suddenly endangered. But the judge picked up the control cup and turned it in his hands.

"Tell me about this one," she said.

"It gets no change at all," Luca said. "Plain water, same light, same everything. The tested groups only make sense if I can compare them against it."

The judge nodded slowly and wrote something on her clipboard. "Most students forget that part," she said, and moved on.

Marcus clapped him on the shoulder. "So the dead-looking plant is actually your best one."

"It's the most important one," Luca said. He watered all nine cups, saving the control for last, and straightened its sticky note so the word Water faced the aisle.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Line dances, in which a group repeats the same set of steps facing the same direction, let people dance together without needing a partner.
story:
Maeva stood in the kitchen with one sock on the tile and one bare foot in the air, frozen mid-step. The school dance was in three hours, and she had a problem with a name: Daniel Okafor. He'd asked her, she'd said yes, and then he'd texted, "Actually I don't know how to dance with a partner. Sorry." She'd stared at the phone so long her mom asked if the screen was broken.

"It's not broken," Maeva said. "It's just wrong."

Her little brother Theo, who had recently convinced Dad to install a basketball hoop over the garage door, was dribbling a ball against the refrigerator. "Dances are controversial anyway," he said. "Jayden says you have to hold a girl's hand and it's a hygiene hazard."

"You don't know anything."

"I know you're standing on one foot."

She put her foot down. Then she picked up her phone again, not for Daniel's text, but to search. Last summer at the community picnic she'd seen everybody from grandmas to six-year-olds doing the same steps in rows, and nobody had seemed paired up. She found a video from the picnic and watched it twice. Every person faced the same way, toward the picnic table with the lemonade. Every person repeated the same set of steps, over and over, a grapevine to the right, a clap, a stomp, a quarter turn. Nobody touched anybody. She tested her idea right there on the kitchen tile: she followed along, stumbled, tried again, and by the fourth repeat her feet knew the pattern without her watching.

"Whoa," Theo said. "What's that?"

"It's called a line dance," Maeva said. "A whole group does the same steps, facing the same direction, and you don't need a partner at all."

"Prove it."

She held out her hand for the ball, set it on the counter, and started the video from the beginning. "Just copy me." Theo knocked over a chair on the grapevine and laughed so hard he missed the clap, but on the second run he made it all the way to the quarter turn. On the third run they did it without the video, both facing the window, both stomping at the same moment.

At the dance, the gym was hot and loud and half the seventh grade stood along the wall like wallpaper. Daniel was there, arms crossed, alone. Maeva took a breath, walked over, and said, "You don't need a partner. You just need about four steps. Watch my feet."

The DJ started a song with a beat she knew. She stepped out onto the floor, faced the stage, and began.

"Like this?" Daniel said, two beats behind her.

"Just like that."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: Compound interest is paid on the principal plus all the interest already earned, so the interest itself starts earning interest.
story:
Elliot stared at the two columns Mr. Ruiz had taped to the whiteboard, and both looked exactly the same to him. By Friday, every sixth grader had to bring in a chart comparing what fifty dollars would become in a savings account after five years, and Mr. Ruiz had made it clear he would call on people at random to explain the difference between simple and compound interest. Elliot's chart showed the simple kind: two dollars fifty each year, added up again and again, until his pencil marks marched across the page in a flat, even line. The compound column was the one that made no sense to him.

"It's like this," said Maya, dropping into the seat beside him. She opened her notebook to a page covered in tiny sketches of paintbrushes. "The compound one goes up faster. Look, here, and here, and here." Her finger tapped the gaps, which grew wider every year. Maya wanted the class prize, a twenty-five-dollar bookstore gift card, because she'd been saving all fall for a real set of watercolors and was still nine dollars short. A gift card would finish it.

"That's what my dilemma is," Elliot said. "If both accounts pay the same percent, why does one end up with more? It's like the money is growing on money that didn't exist yet." He copied both columns onto graph paper, and then, because he wanted to clarify it for himself, he wrote out every single interest payment, year by year, for both accounts. The simple payments never changed: two dollars fifty, two dollars fifty, two dollars fifty. The compound payments did. Three dollars twelve. Three dollars ninety. Each one bigger than the last, even though nobody ever added a penny to the account.

"Wait," Maya said, leaning over his page. "Say that part again."

"The interest payments themselves got bigger," Elliot said slowly, reading his own numbers. "Even though we added nothing." He underlined the column where each new payment was calculated on the principal plus all the interest already earned, so the interest itself started earning interest. That was the rule. That was the whole difference. The simple account only ever paid on the original fifty, which was why its line lay flat as a ruler while the compound line bent slowly upward.

On Thursday night Maya left a folded note in his locker: "I showed my cousin the chart and she says we're right. She has a savings account and one year her interest payment grew a little even though she added nothing to the account. Want to present together tomorrow? P.S. The art store closes at six on Saturdays." The hallway around the lockers felt almost desolate at that hour, empty and echoing, but Elliot read the note twice and grinned at the ceiling both times.

On Friday they stood at the front with their chart, and when Mr. Ruiz called on Maya to explain the compound column, she pointed at the growing payments and said, "Each one is paid on the principal plus all the interest already earned, so the interest itself starts earning interest." Mr. Ruiz wrote a big check mark on his clipboard. When the bell rang, Maya held up the gift card they'd split toward the watercolors and said, "Saturday, nine a.m., art store. You're carrying the paint."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: In the United States, a large CDC survey found the median age of a girl's first period is about 12 years old, with a wide normal range around it.
story:
The last three gummy bears in the bag dwindled to two, then one, and then just a red smudge on Maya's thumb while she stared out the window of the minivan. Her mom was driving them to Priya's house for a sleepover, and her little brother, Theo, was conducting his own campaign from the back seat. "Can we listen to my dinosaur podcast? Please? I've been waiting all week."

"One episode," Mom said, "after Maya tells me why she's smiling at her phone like that."

Maya wasn't smiling at her phone exactly. She was smiling at a thought. Last weekend at Priya's house, Priya had mentioned that her older sister got her first period at fourteen, which had surprised them both, because Zoe's older sister had gotten hers at eleven. Fourteen and eleven. That was a pretty big spread, and Maya couldn't stop wondering about it. Was there a normal age, or was it all just random? She couldn't see the answer anywhere, but maybe she could find it hiding in the pattern, the way you figure out a rule in math class.

So she had made a survey. She had texted ten friends and asked, "How old was your mom or your sister when she got her first period?" The replies had rolled in all afternoon: eleven, thirteen, twelve, fourteen, ten, twelve, eleven, fifteen, twelve, thirteen. Maya counted them twice on the van's armrest. Four of them were twelve, which was more than any other number, so the middle of the pile sat right there. But the edges stretched all the way from ten to fifteen. There was a center, and there was a range around it, wide as a river.

"Mom," Maya said, leaning between the seats, "when you were a kid, did anyone ever tell you the usual age for getting your first period?"

Mom glanced in the mirror. "My health teacher said something once, but I don't remember it. Why?"

"Priya's sister told her that some big CDC survey found the median age is about twelve," Maya said, "with a wide normal range around it. And guess what my survey says."

"Twelve?" Mom guessed.

"Twelve, with a range from ten to fifteen." Maya held up her phone like evidence in court. "My own data matches a giant government survey. Ten whole people." She felt a little thrill, like she had pulled back a curtain on something invisible. Her own body hadn't started yet, and somehow that felt less like being behind and more like being somewhere inside a wide, ordinary river.

Theo tugged her sleeve. "Enough period talk. Dinosaurs. Now."

"One episode," Mom said, laughing, and pressed play.

Theo leaned back, triumphant, and Maya gave his rebellious, podcast-demanding hand a pat. "Fine," she said, "but when it's over, I'm telling you about medians. It's basically the T. rex of numbers."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: The earliest eyeglasses were made in central Italy around 1290.
story:
Kaylee sat on the crackly paper of the exam chair and stared at the chart across the room, where the third line had gone soft and blurry no matter how hard she squinted. The optometrist swung a heavy metal machine in front of her face and clicked lenses into it, one after another. "Better or worse?" she kept asking, and each time Kaylee answered, the world sharpened a little more. When the chair sank with a hiss, Kaylee glanced down and saw a small brass valve on the side, the kind that let air or fluid in and out. The optometrist must have noticed her looking, because she said, "Handy, right? I can lower it for kids and raise it back for adults."

In the frame room afterward, Kaylee tried on pair after pair while her mom watched from a stool by the window. Everything was too big, too round, or too much like something a grandmother would wear. Finally she found a thin wire pair with purple at the hinges, and the optician said they were titanium, durable enough to survive being dropped, which mattered, because Kaylee dropped things constantly.

"These are the ones," she said, turning her head in the little mirror. Then a thought hit her so hard she said it out loud. "Wait. What did people do before glasses existed? Like, in ancient times? Everyone who couldn't see just... couldn't read?"

The optician hummed and straightened a display of cases. "Well, glasses weren't actually that old an invention, if you think about it. The earliest eyeglasses were made in central Italy, around 1290."

"Thirteen ninety?" Kaylee said, gripping the mirror's edge.

"Twelve ninety. Central Italy."

Kaylee did the math, and the math made her dizzy. People had been writing things down for thousands of years before that, and for most of that time, anyone with eyes like hers would have had to hold a page practically against her nose, or give up entirely. She began to elaborate her theory out loud: that must be why some old paintings showed scholars holding books at arm's length, or squinting like she did at the whiteboard last Tuesday when she copied the homework wrong and got a zero she didn't deserve. That zero was the reason she was here. She'd spent a month blaming the teacher's handwriting before admitting the real cause was hiding behind her own eyeballs, invisible until she finally tested the idea by sitting in the front row and getting everything right.

"So for thousands of years," she said slowly, "everyone who needed glasses just didn't get any."

Her mom came over and rested a hand on her shoulder. "And now you do. That's something."

The optician slid the purple-hinged pair into a case and wrote the pickup date on a slip. "Next Thursday, after school."

Kaylee folded the slip into her pocket, right next to the crumpled zero she'd kept as evidence.

"Thursday," she said. "I'm going to see everything."
